data.text:
Geopolitics demands that we see the world as it is. Not the world as it was, nor the world as others want us to see it.

Modern-day Japan is not the Empire of Japan.

The People’s Republic of China is not Nationalist China.

While these ancient nations claim continuity of civilization into antiquity, modern polities must be judged by modern actions. 

The atrocities committed by Imperial Japan are indisputable. In Singapore, the scars of the Japanese Occupation endure. Sook Ching, the massacre of between five to twenty-five thousand people in 1942, remains the deadliest mass killing in Singapore history.

Recently, when PM Lawrence Wong made comments critical of China during its dispute with Japan, online voices started piling on him, invoking the horrors of the Occupation. I can sympathise. 

In 1947, most of the perpetrators of Sook Ching were tried and either hanged or imprisoned for life. In 1966, Japan agreed to pay $50 million as ‘a gesture of atonement’, not as ‘damages’ or ‘reparations’. To date, Japan has not issued a formal apology. The decades-only grievance still lingers among many Singaporeans.
Yet modern Japan is not Imperial Japan.

After World War Two, Japan renounced war. Japan has started no wars. Japan deployed troops overseas only under the auspices of the United Nations, or for noncombat duties. Instead, Japan rebuilt itself into a global economic powerhouse, prioritising industrialization, trade and partnership. The Empire died in atomic fire; from the ashes emerged a new Japan.

We cannot say the same for the People’s Republic of China.

Today, China pursues grey zone warfare. Chinese distant-water fishing fleets ravage exclusive economic zones from Ecuador to West Africa to the Galápagos, violating the sovereignty of small states. Using debt-trap diplomacy, China extracts leverage across Africa, Asia, Europe and Latin America, seizing control of strategic ports.

Beijing orders the Chinese Maritime Militia to harass foreign ships in contested areas, then denies government control when confronted. Domestic nationalism is mobilised to pressure adversaries following a clash between CMM and foreign vessels. China asserts ‘indisputable sovereignty’ over ninety percent of the South China Sea, defying a 2016 PCA ruling, while building militarized artificial islands in the Spratlys. 

When challenged on its claims, China falls back to its narrative of being a victim of the Century of Humiliation or Japanese war crimes. Yet it is the same China that is now building specialized barges designed for large-scale amphibious landings in Taiwan. Chinese influencers and elites are openly discussing reunifying Taiwan and taking over the Ryukyus and claiming Palawan. 

This is China today.

Singapore, far from China and Japan, may appear insulated from great power disputes. Some may believe Singapore has the option of neutrality. This is not the case. 

Consider the unthinkable: what if China attempts to force reunification with Taiwan within the next five to ten years?

Here is a possible sequence of events:

Beijing imposes a blockade on Taiwan. Taiwan manufactures over 60% of the world’s semiconductors, and 90% of the advanced ones. This will shock Singapore’s semiconductor, electronics, and precision engineering sectors within weeks. If Singapore issues a protest, China could retaliate through boycotts and propaganda. 

Of the nearly one million foreign nationals resident in Taiwan, 94% are Southeast Asians. Singapore, as ASEAN’s most capable logistics hub and the only member with strategic air- and sealift capabilities, would likely be called upon to coordinate or lead a non-combatant evacuation operation—potentially the largest in history.

If the blockade escalates into open warfare and the United States commits to defending Taiwan, then China will attempt to neutralise or suppress US forces in Okinawa and sever Japan’s air and sea lines of communication. This will inevitably draw Japan into the war. China’s assassin’s mace doctrine involves employing missile strikes, cyber warfare, electromagnetic pulse weapons, and antisatellite attacks to degrade U.S. and Japanese command, control, and infrastructure within the initial hours of conflict. This could include widespread power outages, destruction of military satellites, and disabling critical communications and Internet infrastructure.

The Singapore Armed Forces may be called upon to evacuate nearly one million civilians amidst a warzone, with no guarantees of ceasefires to protect noncombatants, much less non-belligerents. 

The asymmetry between China and Singapore is absolute: the Chinese military can strike at Singapore, but Singapore’s cannot meaningfully retaliate against the Chinese mainland.

China’s Rocket Force fields thousands of conventional ballistic and cruise missiles. Missile units in Hainan can range the South China Sea and beyond. Singapore itself is within range of the DF-26 ballistic missile. A strike package of several hundred missiles is within the capabilities of the People’s Liberation Army. Singapore has no such strike capability.

In a prolonged conflict, the rest of ASEAN will be dragged into the war. US forces in the region will be Chinese targets. For example, American forces and contractors operate out of five military facilities in the northern Philippines. These bases are within Chinese missile range. 

Singapore hosts the headquarters of the US Navy’s Task Force 73 / Commander, Logistics Group Western Pacific. In a Taiwan shooting war, these facilities would become the primary logistics node for the US Seventh Fleet. Regardless of Singapore’s stance, like with the Philippines, this alone will place Singapore in the crosshairs. 

A Chinese operation to destroy TF 73 may look like this:

D-30 to D-5: Cyber intrusions, satellite overpasses, and spy ship reconnaissance to map SAF air defence sites and US facilities.

D-3 to D-1: Submarines and dark fleet civilian vessels seed thousands of mines across the Straits of Singapore and Malacca as well as RSN patrol boxes. 

H-12 to H-1: Chinese forces launch a diversionary attack, drawing off US Navy assets from Singapore.

H-0: H-6K strategic bombers launch TL-30 anti-radiation missiles against SAF air defence radars and missiles. DF-26 and DF-21 missile barrages target piers, fuel depots, command nodes, and ships. Intense cyber and electronic warfare blinds surviving sensors.

H+6 to H+48: Battle damage assessment and follow-on strikes. Naval mines activate, enforcing a de facto blockade. 

A salvo of 150 to 300 missiles is likely to saturate Singapore’s Aster-30 and SPYDER air defence systems. Clearing thousands of naval mines could take weeks or months. 

This, of course, represents the worst-case scenario. Chinese forces will likely focus on Guam and Okinawa. But should the worst come to pass, a strike could disrupt the economy and drag Singapore into a superpower conflict. A responsible government must account for this situation.

Since its founding, Singapore has been fortunate to avoid major wars. But a prolonged Taiwan conflict will drag Singapore into a superpower showdown. 

Singapore cannot hope that China’s affection for its diaspora will stay its hand. China already has the means to strike Singapore to hinder US operations. For China, such a strike is merely a question of political calculus and military strategy.  Likewise, Singapore cannot hope that China will fight according to the Western ways of war, in obedience to Western moral norms. 

As Neville Chamberlain discovered in 1939, and Ukraine learned in 2014 and 2022, appeasement does not work. Singaporeans cannot hope that by the appeasing the dragon, the dragon will not turn its teeth on Singapore.

 Dragons will do what dragons have always done. As a small country, Singapore cannot confront a dragon alone. What it can do is support those who can confine it to its cave. This means upholding international law and supporting powers capable of checking China’s ambitions, while carefully managing relations with neighbours and trade partners. Even if it means occasionally making political incorrect statements, this is what Singapore must do. Singapore cannot pretend that a roaring dragon is a sleeping panda.

We must honour the ghosts of 1942, but the policies of 2025 must be decided by the living and for the living, looking at the world as it is—not as it was.
